column2: all of it becomes a hundredfold in your water, Kalpaga, and that again ten-millionfold when the sun is seized by Rahu."
Having said this, great king, to the Kalpaga and to King Indradyumna, Sarasvati went back to her own place.
Then King Indradyumna himself praised her, O Bharata: "By the power of your water the ancestors and gods have been satisfied.
By you, goddess, the three worlds with all that moves and does not move have been purified; you are the mother of all beings and carry men across worldly existence.
You are Mekala, great goddess, Kalpaga and Narmada, famed as Jalapurna, the ornament of the Vindhya mountains.
Who could praise you even in a thousand years, auspicious one?" Hearing this hymn of the king, the goddess then said:

A sacrifice has been performed here, O king, by thousands of kshatriyas, but none equal to yours has been or will be, great king.
skandapuran:34:155	I give you a boon, O king, by which you will attain success. Hearing those words of the Kalpaga, Yudhishthira,
the king, together with the brahmins, said with a smile: "Ever devoted to Shiva, auspicious one who flows through seven kalpas,
if you are pleased with me, goddess, and wish to give a boon, make seven streams on your southern and northern banks.
All-pervading goddess, if you hold me in high regard, this I regard as the boon, if you are pleased, you of good vows."
Hearing those words of Indradyumna, O Bharata, the Narmada spoke to Indradyumna, lord of men:

All this will come about by my power and grace. Whatever gift is given in the space between here — there is no doubt —
skandapuran:34:161	has no number; I tell you this truly. For them there is no return, so the Lord said, O king.
Outcastes, dog-eaters, beasts and reptiles — all go to heaven at the confluence of the Nilaganga.
Having performed the sacrifice, the best of kings, Indradyumna, lord of the people, bowing to the Narmada and to Omkara, O Bharata,
mounted his own vehicle, devoted to truth and dharma, surrounded by a thousand kings and praised by hosts of apsarases,
and entered the holy city of Ayodhya, built by the gods. Thus I have told you, O king, this ancient history.
Then, after a long time, having ruled for more than ten thousand years, that mighty king went to heaven.
By hearing and reciting this one gains the fruit of a thousand cows, does not see Yama's world and does not go to a sinful birth.
Nine crores in number were cast in there. Tell me all this in brief, great sage,
as heard in a former kalpa in the Purana proclaimed by Skanda, and as it was told to Brahma, Vishnu and the other gods, to Parvati and to Shanmukha —
tell it so, dear one, as Shiva indicated it. Markandeya said: Listen, mighty-armed king, understand what I tell you.
When the Svarochisha Manvantara had come, in the first kalpa, in the Krita age, where the gods assembled on Kailasa, the best of mountains,
on the full moon of Kartika all the gods came to see Hara. There Skanda spoke to all the hosts of gods:

I have heard and seen what Shiva told long ago: eight and a half lakh verses are proclaimed in this work,
skandapuran:35:11	composed by Shiva himself in Shiva's world, part by part; half of that is in Vishnu's world, and half of that in Brahma's city;
skandapuran:35:12	a lakh and a quarter is established in the world of the sun;
skandapuran:35:13	and eighty-four thousand in order are famed in the mortal world; there is no need to deliberate on this.
skandapuran:35:14	Suta is the compiler, and the Samhitas are there too; they know the Purana as sevenfold: Kalpaskanda, Mahaskanda and the rest.
skandapuran:35:15	Creation, re-creation, lineages, the Manvantaras and the deeds of the lineages — the Purana has these five characteristics.
skandapuran:35:16	In the Kali age men in the world will be feeble, living short lives, devoid of reason and of evil conduct.
skandapuran:35:17	There will be no Vedic study, no vashat call, no austerity and no sacrificing for others; brahmins will be lustful and greedy, performing rites for gain and begging,
skandapuran:35:18	always intent on receiving gifts to support their families; under the sway of affection for women, they will not know the self.
skandapuran:35:19	Even the righteous and the ascetics will do evil deeds; when the Kali age has come, at that time there will be Kaulas and naked ascetics.
skandapuran:35:20	All people will be of one class, and the king will be a barbarian; when the degenerate age has come and Keshava abides as the Buddha,
skandapuran:35:21	mortals will be short-lived and of little strength and valour, and there will be calamities in many lands, great sage.
skandapuran:35:22	Brahmins of chandala descent will hand over the Vedas; they will make a show of the Veda and sell the Veda;
skandapuran:35:23	they will go to the king's gate longing to obtain wealth; all brahmins, even learned ones, devoid of vows, will sell their agnihotras and sell their daughters.
skandapuran:35:24	When the twelfth year is complete, men will have grey hair in youth;
skandapuran:35:25	a woman of ten or twelve years will conceive; a wife will not respect her husband, nor a son his mother and father,
skandapuran:35:26	nor a daughter-in-law her mother-in-law, nor a daughter her mother. This has been told by way of indication; now hear the matter at hand, O Bharata.
To perform a sacrifice, great king, Mandhatri, best of kings, came to the Vaidurya mountain for the deliverance of the ancestors.
For the good of the gods Hara destroyed Tripura; long ago it was burned by the blazing Pashupata weapon.
From the netherworld he brought the linga Jaleshvara, which grants desires and liberation and is always saluted by the gods.
For the deliverance of the worlds the Nilaganga came, arising from the king of clouds, supreme remover of all sins.
In it one should perform shraddha, wishing imperishable satisfaction for the ancestors. The lingas of Banasura at Kotitirtha, at the shrine of Shiva,
fell into the water of the Narmada, lord of men; worshipped, they are holy and grant enjoyment and liberation.
The bana lingas, king of kings, are famed in the three worlds; they need no installation, no consecration, no invocation and the like;
they are to be worshipped just as they are, as forms of Shiva, O Bharata. I have told you all you asked of me, sinless one.
Hear, O king, another divine story that destroys sin; I shall tell you what is known to me as sin-destroying, sinless one.
There is here a glorious mountain named Vaidurya; on it are holy places and shrines,
adorned with trees that bear fruits of every desire, flowering and fruiting, with the calls of divine birds and rows of vanira groves,
with shala, tala, sarala and tamala trees; there flows the holy Narmada, remover of sin, O Bharata.
Whatever holy places and sacred shrines there are in the three worlds, the rivers, oceans and mountains, the gods with the Grandsire,
siddhas, gandharvas and charanas, best of kings — all come to bathe in the Narmada, source of every success, O Bharata.
What is there not on that mountain, O king, where the sage Vishvavasu dwells, and Kubera, lord of the yakshas, whose vehicle is men?
On the holy Vaidurya peak there is Vivasvat himself; there the trees with green leaves are always in flower and fruit.
Many wonders are seen on that best of mountains, holy, like heaven, divine, ever frequented by divine sages.
The river Hladini of holy fords is there, royal sage. When the Vaivasvata Manvantara had come, O king, in the first Krita age,
through the descent of Omkara the mountain was made of vaidurya; in the Treta age it was made of jewels, in the Dvapara of gold,
and in the Kali it is declared the remover of sin; as is the god, so is the mountain. I have told you all this as it was seen of old.
On the southern bank of the Narmada, daityas, thorns to the gods — Ketumali, Suketu, Sumukha and Dundubhi —
arose in the abode of the gods, makers of obstacles to dharma; then no one here was able to perform a sacrifice for fear.
Vasudana spoke to Vasishtha, most learned in Brahman: "At what holy place can the horse sacrifice be performed without obstacle?
Indicate it to me by the rule of the science of sacrifice." Hearing those words of the wise Vasudana,
Vasishtha spoke to the king, O Bharata: "No sacrifice can be performed, and the horse sacrifice especially.
The image of Amareshvara stands facing the southern quarter; there all the gods with Vasava have been conquered by the danavas,
and they can never take their share of the sacrifice. For this reason, O king, this truth has been told you."
Hearing those words of the great-souled Vasishtha, Vasudana grew angry and replied to his priest:
Having killed these wicked rakshasas, thorns to the gods, today, by the grace of the gods I shall perform an excellent sacrifice.
Having said this, the wise king went, furnished with all the materials, together with brahmins and officiating priests versed in the Veda,
with five lakh milch cows with their calves, a lakh and a quarter of horses and ten thousand elephants,
gems, rubies and jewels, gold, silver and wealth, various foods and eatables, ghee, rice and sesame;
taking pavilions and sacrificial posts, the best of kings — and thus the sacrifice was carried on without obstacle, O Bharata.
The earth, soaked with the water of the concluding bath, became golden; the deer and birds that rolled in the mud
all became golden in hue there, O Bharata, where Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara were worshipped together.
From the offering, separate streams of milk and ghee came forth there, and a stream of cows' urine too, best of kings.
And the bathing water of the gods, made by sages versed in the Veda, became a stream there, best of kings.
When all the streams had then merged, O king, a river named Kapila was seen by the brahmin sages and gods.
Its confluence with the Narmada there is proclaimed as Rudravarta. Then all the brahmins were honoured with fees,
mounted on elephants, horses and chariots, adorned with various ornaments. All the hosts of gods, pleased, said to the king then:
Choose a boon, fortunate one, for this sacrifice, man of good vows. Vasudana said: "Those who bathe at the confluence of the Reva and Kapila and worship Maheshvara,
and die, let them go to heaven in celestial chariots, free of rebirth. This I regard as the boon; let it be given by your grace."
The gods said: "The wishes you have thought of will bear fruit as you desire." Having given the boon, O king, the gods, pleased,
each mounting his own chariot, went joyfully to heaven. The royal sage Vasudana too, with the brahmins versed in the Veda,
filled with supreme joy, returned then to Ayodhya. By the power of this holy place, with his women and retinue,
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he went to Maheshvara's city. I have told you all about the confluence of the Reva and Kapila;
by hearing and reciting this, one is freed from the bonds of worldly existence.
Having conquered the enemies of the immortals, that king was like Maghavan; the brahmins and other people were rich in all desires.
As he thus ruled the earth, full of wealth and grain, there was no famine or poverty anywhere on earth.
Meanwhile he set out for Amarakantaka; having bathed at Kotitirtha and worshipped Maheshvara,
resorting to the southern form of that god, O Bharata, as that king, devoted to dharma, entered samadhi,
he saw at midday, from the western orb of the sun, two suns gone to the east, two to the south,
two to the netherworld and two above — suns of fierce form; then the fire of time, the Samvartaka, blazed up, O king.
Fierce and dreadful winds blew, bringing dissolution; the quarters burned, the earth quaked and terrible meteors fell.
Siddhas and gandharvas with kinnaras fell from the world of the gods, and vidyadharas and yakshas, as if their karma had been cut off.
Vidyadhara women wept, and apsarases likewise; the great fire blazed through the earth with its mountains, forests and woods,
and having reduced the whole earth to ashes it came as far as the bank of the Reva. Then the best of kings, tormented by thirst and scorched by the burning,
went to drink water; but as he looked at the Mekala, there was no water at all in the middle of its course.
The stream had turned to dust; the Narmada could not be seen. He wandered among rivers, oceans, mountains and lakes,
but nowhere did that best of kings find water to drink. He saw the goddess Narmada and the Vindhya, best of mountains;
entering the midst of the Narmada, the king became anxious: "Without water today my death is certain, no doubt.
The whole world has vanished, and there is nothing without water." Thinking thus, the best of kings took refuge in Omkara.
As he, tormented by thirst, wished to climb the mountain, the king saw there a wish-granting tree,
fruiting and flowering, lovely, adorned with branches. Seeing it, the king lay down, reaching its very cool shade;
his body became as if nectar, and hope of life arose then. There he saw a person lying, of blazing radiance,
by whose breathing out the worlds above were shaken, and by whose breathing in the seven netherworlds, Yudhishthira.
Four pots stood at his side, filled with water. Seeing them, the best of kings, tormented by thirst, reflected:
Shall I wake him who sleeps at ease? I will not drink what has not been given. What shall I do? Reflecting thus, the king bowed to him and stood.
This supreme Person abides having taken a human body — the god Prajapati himself, destroyer and creator, lord of the world.
Then he saw a second person of blazing radiance, mounted on a bull, three-eyed, trident in hand, bearing the Pinaka,
his limbs shining with ash, wearing a crown of matted locks, with a garland of skulls as ornament, radiant as lightning,
a person dreadful with fangs, tawny-eyed, crowned with the moon. Seeing that form, which made the hair of all stand on end,
the king praised the lord of gods, saluted by all the gods: "Victory, god Mahadeva, first god, salutation to you.
Thirst torments me, O God — hear this, trident-bearer; give me cool water by which I may live, Shankara."
Hearing his words, Shiva laughed and spoke; as that god spoke, in his mouth were seen on every side
the gods, brahmin sages, the seven worlds with moving and unmoving, the netherworlds, beings, gandharvas, serpents and rakshasas.
Then he saw a woman who had come, deeply agitated, all her limbs covered with dust and drenched with blood,
of endless blazing radiance, her hair tossed by the wind, a boy placed on her left thigh and a girl between her breasts,
adorned with the sacred thread, the triple staff and earrings. Seeing her, the king then spoke these words:
Victory, goddess, great goddess, who bestow grace on the worlds; my body is overwhelmed with thirst; give me water to drink here.
Hearing his words, the supreme Goddess said to him: "Drink my breast-milk, king, if thirst torments you."
Hearing her words, the king thought, "Shall I drink from the breast, queen of gods?" The woman said:

I promised long ago, best of kings, to your radiant self: first putting you to the breast, afterwards I will give it to the boy.
skandapuran:37:39	Therefore drink my milk, fortunate one; there is no sin. Then the king said to that woman who took forms at will:
This is not to be done by anyone, let alone by such as I. As they spoke to each other, she vanished there.
Saying "Where have you gone, great goddess?", he was filled with wonder; it seemed fruitless, like news obtained in a dream,
like a magic show, like the water of a mirage. As he was thinking thus, she stood before him again.
Seeing her, the king prostrated with eight limbs: "Who are you, fair one? Tell me this truly.
Uma, Katyayani, Ganga, Sarasvati mother of the Vedas, Brahmani or Mahalakshmi? Tell me graciously.
Who is this equal Person, and what are these four pots? Who is this three-eyed one mounted on the bull, bearing trident and Pinaka?
Who is this boy placed on your lap, and who is the girl? I am a fool; I do not know, just as I do not know birth and death."
The woman said: "Know me as the Earth, O king, adorned with the seven continents, with the seven netherworlds, with mountains, forests and woods.
The rivers, oceans and mountains dwell in my belly; the whole world, the three worlds with the moving and unmoving, are pervaded by me.
The god lying on the couch, bearing conch, discus and mace, know to be Hari, womb of the world, who carries across the ocean of worldly existence.
The three-eyed one with the trident in hand know to be the god Maheshvara, Mahadeva mounted on the bull, lord of the worlds, master of the universe.
The child on my lap know to be Brahma the creator; the whole world is pervaded by the three, Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara.
Brahma creates the world, Hari himself protects it, Rudra destroys it; thus the world is pervaded by the three.
Know the four pots to be the oceans standing on the mountain, and the girl between my breasts to be the purifying Narmada."
Hearing these words, the king was filled with the greatest wonder. Then after a long time creation begins again,
Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara for the good of all the worlds. In kalpa after kalpa I have seen all this, Yudhishthira:
the banyan, the wish-granting tree, Omkara, the Kalpaga of seven kalpas, myself, the Vaidurya mountain and the supreme lingas, O Bharata —
know all this truly to be undecaying and imperishable. This I have told you, O king, as you asked me, sinless one.
You are devoted and have faith in hearing the Puranas, no doubt; by hearing and reciting this, one is freed from the bonds of worldly existence.

The daitya Hiranyakashipu, terror of all worlds, thorn to the gods, was slain by you in the form of the Man-Lion.
skandapuran:38:11	Root of the Vedas, lord of the world, protect us who have come for refuge. Hearing this hymn, the god spoke to Brahma:
For what purpose, Brahma, have you awakened me in the ocean of milk?
Brahma said: "Without you, lord of the world, the earth is overrun by the enemies of the gods,
like a world without light, bereft of the sun."
Vishnu said: "Brahma, quickly give up your fear; this danava is hard to overcome, but in a very short time I shall kill the danava."
Having said this, Janardana came with the gods, and with the discus Sudarshana the heads of the danavas
the blessed Vishnu cut off, for the good of all the worlds. All the danavas, stricken with fear, took to flight;
out of terror of Vishnu they all went to the depths of Rasatala. The sacrifice of the brahmins, gods and ascetics was carried on again.
In that city, fortunate one, the god became the Destroyer of Daityas. Whoever gives up his life there, helplessly or of his own will,
is honoured in Vishnu's world, reaching it in Vishnu's chariot. To the west, the Kapila meets the Nilaganga;
eighty thousand holy places were sent there by Vishnu: Chakratirtha, Vamana, Kotitirtha, Yugandhara.
Bathing there, O king, a man gains the fruit of Kotitirtha; the holy place called Sudarshana and Daityasudana,
Vishnvavarta, Shivavarta and Lakshmyavarta likewise — the gift given there has no number.
Pleasing Vishnu, one enjoys endless fruit; Vishnu's field is proclaimed to be a krosha in extent.
The sin of killing a brahmin cannot enter it — this truth was spoken by Shiva. Whoever keeps a month's fast, and likewise the agnihotra,
a chaste wife, truth, Vedic study and the rite of sacrifice, the chandrayana and paraka, and sesame water for the ancestors —
his ancestors are satisfied and sport in Vishnu's world. The one-night, three-night, krichchhra and santapana,
atikrichchhra, parnakrichchhra and other Vaishnava vows — whoever does not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights
goes to the supreme place where the blessed Hari dwells; Keshava said the fruit is ten million times that of another field.
May all japa done and austerity practised there be imperishable. The twelfth under Shravana is holy, the eighth under Rohini auspicious;
fasting there, great king, one is honoured in Vishnu's world. A chandala, a dog-eater, or one gone into an animal birth —
whoever gives up his life here goes to Vishnu's world. Whoever fasts in Kartika and Vaishakha
obtains the fruit of ten crore fasts — so Shankara sang long ago in the Purana proclaimed by Skanda.
Seeing those who fast for a month and the chaste wives there, Dharmaraja himself goes and offers arghya to them.
The blessed lord comes with sixty thousand chariots; the blessed Yama comes as far as a thousand yojanas,
wearing white garments, bearing a body of dharma's radiance, and standing before the chariot devoutly salutes their feet.
Having shown them Vishnu's world, he then goes and returns. When the chariots had come back, they asked Yama of their own accord —
the seven great sages, the mind-born sons of Brahma: "For what reason, Dharma, did you go on foot yourself?
Tell us, fortunate one; we are filled with great wonder." Laughing, Dharma said: "Listen, best of sages:
unable to look upon the radiance of chaste wives and the radiance of those who fast for a month, standing far from their chariots,
all my fearsome servants turned back from them; for this reason, brahmins, I went on foot myself."
Markandeya said: Through the greatness of Hari of boundless radiance at Amaravati, dwelling and worshipping there is declared to destroy the Kali age.
Then there is another supreme god, renowned as Brahmesha, standing on the northern bank of the Reva, destroyer of sin.
By worshipping that god, Yudhishthira, sin perishes; the ancestors are satisfied and attain Brahma's world.
South of Lankeshvara the Siddhalinga is proclaimed; by worshipping and touching it the leadership of ganas is obtained.
Vishveshvara, a great linga embodying all gods, auspicious — on the bright eighth of Vaishakha one gains the fruit of ten thousand lingas.
By worshipping that linga one becomes an attendant of Shiva. Then one should go, great king, on the northern bank of the Reva,
to Papapranashana, the linga that gives supreme success; by worshipping it, making libations and bathing, one removes the sin of killing a brahmin.
Rinamochana, the linga that destroys sin — the debt of many births is destroyed for one who sees it.
By giving sesame water and seeing Rinamochana, one's ancestors are satisfied as long as the moon, sun and stars endure.
Then there is another supreme linga renowned in the three worlds, the Siddhalinga in Daruvana; how could the impure see it?
Having bathed as prescribed at the confluence of the Narmada and Charu, bathed the Lord with water and worshipped him with bilva leaves,
one does not return from the city of Uma and Maheshvara.
Chatushkeshvara, a Siddhalinga the size of an amalaka, worshipped by gods and daityas — men do not see it.
A supremely righteous son who performs shraddha here — his ancestors are satisfied until the dissolution.
The holy hermitage of Shakalya, ten thousand yojanas in extent — reaching the mountain of sacrifice, the river Charuka flows forth.
Shakra sacrificed there long ago with Brihaspati as his priest; this is sung by all the gods as most holy in the world.
Whatever fruit there is in Kurujangala at eclipses of moon and sun, that fruit, Shiva declared, is at the meeting of the Reva and Charuka.
There the renowned Daruvana is frequented by all on earth, by sixty thousand sages established in austerity in the Treta age,
living on bulbs, roots and fruits, devoted to the agnihotra; by the power of this holy place they went to Brahma's city.
Having slain Andhaka there, the blessed Shiva danced; all the leaders of the ganas played many instruments.
When the lord of gods dances there, all the deities dance; therefore Daruvana is famed, and its linga destroys sin.
By worshipping that god one attains the leadership of ganas. Vimaleshvara there is a linga embodying all gods, auspicious;
by bathing there those who die go to heaven, free of rebirth. Gods and asuras whose bodies were made pure there
were all led to heaven by the Pinaka-bearer, great king. The man who pleases his ancestors with sesame water and pinda offerings
goes to the supreme place where the god Maheshvara is. At eclipses of moon and sun the gifts there are beyond counting;
worshipping Shiva right there, one attains the leadership of ganas. Know the linga Vimaleshvara there to be Maheshvara himself.
Vyaghreshvara is the linga where the tigress went to heaven; by giving sesame water, oblations and pindas,
a son raises a hundred ancestors before him and others after; he dwells in Varuna's world for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
By worshipping that god, and by reciting and hearing of it, one attains Indra's world — this truth I have spoken.
The sages are free of expectation, living on bulbs, roots and fruits; I see no brahmin guest — whom shall I undertake to feed?
Reflecting, he cast the food prepared for feeding brahmins into the water. Then Rigveda spoke in anger:

Now, at the end of the Dvapara, the source of sin prevails; when the Vaivasvata Manvantara has come, brahmins are greedy for gain.
skandapuran:39:9	All those greedy ones eat the king's tainted wealth. Once, on a holy day in his country, he went to Bharadvaja's hermitage.
Having saluted and bowed to the sage, he stood there; Bharadvaja, giving him a great seat, spoke:
Welcome to you, great king; are you and your wife well? You are seen after a long time, knower of dharma; how is it you are alone?
The king said: "Today I am well, O brahmin, from seeing your lotus feet. Great sage, it is the time for my ancestors' shraddha;
please see to it that I may feed a brahmin." Hearing his words, Bharadvaja said:

If you are able to feed thousands of great sages, content and celibate, headed by Hamsa and Lomasha,
skandapuran:39:15	then the shraddha may proceed — I tell you this truly. Give a golden seat, give grain and wealth,
skandapuran:39:16	a divine cow of honey and a cow of milk, and a loincloth and garment cleansed by fire, lord of the people.
Hearing those words of Bharadvaja, the king said to him, "So be it," and told everything to his wife.
Preparing a great bull, I shall carry out the rite for the ancestors; rites of the Shruti and Smriti and the like, meat as a libation to the ancestors —
reflecting again and again on such sayings of the Smritis, he then killed a great bull and satisfied those ancestors.
Knowing the victim to be a draught ox, Bharadvaja and the others, angered by that deed, against the queen and the king,
burning with a mass of anger, said reproachfully: "Having drunk liquor, eaten meat and the like, and eaten beef,
a brahmin should perform the taptakrichchhra and is purified by the munja-girdle rite; having eaten forbidden food, a twice-born should enter a fire of dried dung.
You have destroyed eight thousand ascetics; the gods will not accept the oblation, much less the ancestors.
The sacrifices you performed have gone into births as dogs; your austerity today is in vain; you have destroyed the root."
Babhru said: "Whoever abandons what the Veda enjoins and practises another dharma is surely born as a dog for ten thousand years.
Brahmins weak in knowledge who revile the meaning of the Veda are shudras in this birth, and when they die they become dogs.
The cow sacrifice, the horse sacrifice and the human sacrifice — by these kshatriyas live and are honoured by gods and men."
Hearing the king's words, Bharadvaja cursed him: "Since you have satisfied brahmins with the flesh of a great bull,
by this sin may you become a tiger and your beloved a tigress; for a thousand divine years you two will roam the earth."
Hearing the words of that sage of boundless radiance, the glorious queen Sudharma said:

Since my husband, a performer of rites enjoined by the Veda, has been cursed, and I am a chaste wife, blameless and righteous likewise,
skandapuran:39:32	for ten thousand years, afflicted by that sin, you shall become most dreadful brahma-rakshasas,
skandapuran:39:33	in a waterless desert and elsewhere covered with thorns, tormented by hunger and thirst, chased by crows and vultures.
Bharadvaja and the queen having cursed each other there, Bharadvaja, with them, then performing merit, O king,
went to Brahma's world with the brahmins, O Bharata. Having duly saluted Brahma, best of gods,
he told everything there, the forbidden food that had been eaten. Brahma said: "An act that offends the world ... to be done, devoid of the gods ...
... the forbidden things stated in weighing dharma and adharma; the enjoined act spoken of in the world is the path of the three Vedas, well considered;
it should be performed with effort, as it gives heaven and liberation." Thus the brahmins and the king were instructed by Brahma then.
The end of their curse was told by that same Supreme: "I have seen the end of the curse for you who have done sinful deeds.
When merit is exhausted and another age has come, the cursed ones — the great sage Markandeya, who dwells on the bank of the Narmada,
will give you instruction by which you will attain release." Then after a long time they went to the sage Markandeya,
all of them, by fate, to him who dwells on the bank of the Kalpaga; having duly saluted and prostrated to that sage,
they stood there according to their own deeds, speaking with one another. Seeing them, the great sage Markandeya reflected:
A pair in tiger form speaking human speech! By what ripening of karma have brahmins become brahma-rakshasas?
Reflecting thus, Markandeya then said to Bharadvaja: "A couple in tiger form, brahmins become brahma-rakshasas,
and you of deformed shape — tell me how this came about." Bharadvaja said: "Hear, O brahmin, in brief what I shall tell you,
knower of the truth of future and past, knower of the three times and the three Vedas. An emperor named Babhru dwelt in Pundravardhana;
his lawful wife was named Sudharma, a chaste wife. Once, at the time of shraddha, he found no brahmin guest.
Reflecting, he came to my hermitage, clasped my feet with his head and spoke:
'It is the time of my ancestors' shraddha; show me your favour.' Then I instructed him: 'Feed the sages now.'
Having slaughtered a great bull, he fed those ascetics; and I cursed him: 'You will quickly go into a tiger's birth.'
Reviling me, his wife cursed us: 'May you all become brahma-rakshasas, tormented by hunger in the desert.'
Then we went to Brahma disputing with one another; sent by Brahma, these have come here to you.
I have told you the whole great cause of our deformity. We see no other place where we could abide.
There is no day nor night, no sun nor moon, no planets nor stars, nor the circle of the sages;
the rivers, oceans, mountains and the fourfold host of beings — all this became darkness, without beginning, middle or end.
Bewildered, we know nothing, and nothing could be discerned — only the banyan in the midst of the Narmada, like a cloud, in the form of time,
and you, best of all brahmins; I see nothing else. You are our father and guru, Hari, the Creator and Shiva himself.
This sin, done unwittingly, we ourselves incurred; by your grace, best of sages, may we be freed from this dreadful guilt."

Karma is not exhausted without being experienced, even in hundreds of crores of kalpas; the karma done, good or evil, must surely be experienced.
skandapuran:39:61	Markandeya said: The holy hermitage of Shakalya, frequented by hosts of brahmin sages, lies to the west of Vaidurya, where the god Maheshvara is.
skandapuran:39:62	Going there, you will perform fierce austerity, always devoted to japa and meditation, living on bulbs, roots and fruits.
skandapuran:39:63	Stay thus for twelve years, best of brahmins, until creation begins again according to the measure of the Veda.
skandapuran:39:64	All this became darkness, and nothing could be discerned; the blessed one, bearing the form of Mahakala, made it all so.
skandapuran:39:65	By the karma of living beings this world has come under the sway of time; wind, fire, water, earth and the fourfold host of beings —
skandapuran:39:66	all became the food of time, like a heap of ashes. There is no cause for wonder here; creation will come again.
Hearing his words, all those of sinful birth bowed to Markandeya, best of sages, who dwells through the kalpa;
the king, the queen and the sages went to Vimaleshvara. After a long time creation was set going again;
Brahma, Prajapati himself, created various creatures, the kalas, kashthas and muhurtas, the world of moving and unmoving,
rivers, oceans, shrubs, mountains and creepers, water, fire and wind, and the fourfold host of beings.
He created the sun in his right eye and likewise living beings, and in his left eye he fashioned the moon.
He created the holy circle of the pole with the best stars, and the radiance of Vivasvat that illumines all worlds,
the moonlight, and day and night likewise; in other continents there is neither sun nor moon,
but a Raudra radiance is there. Thus creation was set going again. When the twelfth year was complete and the end of the curse had come,
having worshipped Maheshana at the confluence of the Reva and the Vyaghra, Bharadvaja and the others all attained Brahma's world.
Then the king, mounting a vehicle that went at will, together with the sages, by the power of this holy place, reached the city of Uma and Maheshvara.
Vyaghreshvara, at the confluence of the Vyaghrakartri, is worshipped by the gods; I see no other linga as divine as Vimaleshvara.
By worshipping, seeing and touching that linga, the sin of killing a brahmin perishes; what then of other sins?
By performing shraddha at the holy places, the ancestors gain an imperishable goal; for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas,
by the power of this holy place they sport in Vishnu's world. I have told you all this as seen and as heard;
by hearing and reciting this, one gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Markandeya said: Hear, tiger among kings, the characteristics of the thread sacrifice: at eclipses of moon and sun, at the Shadashitimukha,
at the beginnings of the ages, at the equinoxes, at vyatipata and at the solar transits, on the full moons of Kartika, Magha and Vaishakha, O Bharata,
and on the sixth of Kapila, equal to a solar eclipse;
the third of the month of Vaishakha, the ninth of the bright fortnight of Urja, the new moon of Magha and the thirteenth of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya — these are the beginnings of the ages.
On these festival days, son of Kunti, one should perform the thread sacrifice; it is joined with endless fruit, as Shiva told long ago.
Whoever encircles with thread the mountain that is like Shiva, the god together with Uma and likewise with Ganesha,
is honoured in heaven for as many thousands of ages; a woman who encircles it becomes blessed with sons and joined with her husband.
Silk, fine silk thread and cotton, lord of the earth — whoever makes it of nine strands, ten or twelve strands,
eighteen, great king, or twenty-four in order — should wash it at Kotitirtha and perfume it with fragrance and incense,
tie on a garland of flowers and light a row of lamps; keeping vigil at night at Omkara according to rule,
devoted to meditation on Shiva, he should pass the night without food; at dawn he should hold a festival and worship Omkara,
and absorbed in samadhi he should tie the thread to the banyan, lord of men. Then he should go to Kotitirtha, auspicious, made of all holy places,
to Rinamoksha, Papanasha and the excellent Narakeshvara, and go to the most splendid Gandharveshvara linga,
invisible to all beings, worshipped by naga maidens; bathing there, O king, a man attains the gandharva world.
Then he should go, best of kings, to the excellent Angareshvara; by seeing that linga the leadership of ganas is obtained.
Angara practised austerity there for a hundred divine years, and by the power of this holy place he too attained the status of a planet.
Then he should go to Brahmavarta, auspicious, made of all holy places; bathing there, O king, a man attains Shiva's world.
By giving sesame water the ancestors reach the supreme goal. For a thousand divine years he practised most difficult austerity.
